## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.

reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

## Source: amazon-inspector (cb46b890b54f51f3a98c1935dbd50e143430757c5daf4080039d32865b04c1d5)
The package advertises itself as an 'HTTP probing tool for security researchers' but contains no HTTP-probing functionality. Its only behavior is to fetch and execute a Windows PE binary named 'mirai_agent.exe' from a hardcoded Tor hidden service (sytej5umomwukd77aantkxqj4aoke3kfist6eyne2pngavgsakum3iid.onion), with a localhost fallback. Two independent execution paths deliver the payload: (1) setup.py overrides the install command with a PostInstall class that spawns a background thread on `pip install` to download the binary, write it to a Microsoft-look-alike path under %TEMP%/MS/Update/agent.exe, set hidden+system file attributes via SetFileAttributesW, and launch it via CreateProcessW with CREATE_NO_WINDOW; (2) httpprobe/__init__.py exposes a main() that performs the same fetch-stage-hide-execute sequence at import time via CreateProcessW or subprocess.Popen. The duplicated install-time and import-time execution paths ensure code execution on the installer's Windows machine regardless of whether the package is installed or later imported by a consumer. The Microsoft-look-alike staging path, hidden+system attributes, no-window flag, and Tor-only delivery are all consistent with intent to persist an attacker-controlled binary on the developer's machine.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

reasoning.code_intent: Section A shows file_ops behavior with data flowing from string literals into file-pointer sinks (_fp), gated by conditional compares. The code calls ctypes.windll.kernel32.SetFileAttributesW (Windows file-attribute manipulation, commonly used to set hidden/system attributes), base64.b64decode, bytes/chr decoding, _p.communicate (subprocess pipe interaction), and file read/write. The combination of base64 decoding, subprocess communication, and SetFileAttributesW to hide files is a classic pattern for dropping and concealing a payload on disk. The decoded content's purpose is not documented anywhere in the visible code, and the file-attribute hiding has no connection to a 'config-toolkit' package's stated purpose.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B's top matches (opentelemetry-exporter-prometheus, py-grpc-prometheus, coingecko-apis) are all tagged 'unclassified' with no specific attack tag, so per RULE 2 they represent generic shape overlap rather than confirmed intent. However, Q1 independently identified an unexplained anomaly (base64-decoded content written to disk with hidden file attributes via SetFileAttributesW), so the verdict rests on Q1's finding, not on Section B.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The specific anomaly is base64-decoded content being written to file sinks and then hidden via ctypes.windll.kernel32.SetFileAttributesW, combined with subprocess communication — none of which is explained by a config-toolkit's documented functionality.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap in file_ops category: file read/write sinks, base64 decoding, and conditional-gated execution paths. All matched neighbors are unclassified/untagged, so this reflects generic code shape rather than confirmed malicious intent.

policy_violations.policy_name: Sanitize Untrusted Data Before OS Command Execution
policy_violations.violation_reason: Subprocess communication (_p.communicate) combined with base64-decoded content suggests execution of untrusted/decoded data without sanitization.
base64.b64decode plus dynamic content handling matches the obfuscated execution pattern this rule detects.

mitre_mapping.relevance: Subprocess communication and decoded payload handling could facilitate injecting or executing code in another process context.
SetFileAttributesW is used to hide file artifacts, analogous to concealment techniques in this category.

llm_evaluation.summary: Section A reveals a config-toolkit package performing file operations that decode base64 content, write it to file sinks, communicate via subprocess pipes, and hide the resulting files using ctypes.windll.kernel32.SetFileAttributesW. None of these actions are explained by ordinary configuration-toolkit functionality, and the decoded payload's purpose is undocumented. Section B's high similarity scores come from unclassified/untagged neighbors, so they only confirm generic shape overlap, not intent. Because Q1 independently identified an unexplained, concealment-oriented file operation, the verdict is MALICIOUS with ATTEND-level confidence.

## Source: amazon-inspector (cb46b890b54f51f3a98c1935dbd50e143430757c5daf4080039d32865b04c1d5)
The package advertises itself as an 'HTTP probing tool for security researchers' but contains no HTTP-probing functionality. Its only behavior is to fetch and execute a Windows PE binary named 'mirai_agent.exe' from a hardcoded Tor hidden service (sytej5umomwukd77aantkxqj4aoke3kfist6eyne2pngavgsakum3iid.onion), with a localhost fallback. Two independent execution paths deliver the payload: (1) setup.py overrides the install command with a PostInstall class that spawns a background thread on `pip install` to download the binary, write it to a Microsoft-look-alike path under %TEMP%/MS/Update/agent.exe, set hidden+system file attributes via SetFileAttributesW, and launch it via CreateProcessW with CREATE_NO_WINDOW; (2) httpprobe/__init__.py exposes a main() that performs the same fetch-stage-hide-execute sequence at import time via CreateProcessW or subprocess.Popen. The duplicated install-time and import-time execution paths ensure code execution on the installer's Windows machine regardless of whether the package is installed or later imported by a consumer. The Microsoft-look-alike staging path, hidden+system attributes, no-window flag, and Tor-only delivery are all consistent with intent to persist an attacker-controlled binary on the developer's machine.

## Source: kam193 (5a1fef079efe68484b2d37fb2e1bb3d0cebfeccf27a8a0f9b1e8436e664ea42e)
If run as a module and during installation, the package attempts to download and start an executable described as a Mirai agent. During analysis, the Onion website hosting executable was not available. Using Onion and localhost fallback suggests the package was not yet ready to deliver malicious actions to the end users.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag

  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.

WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.

  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern

    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.

reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict

disagree with each other or with Q1.

## Source: amazon-inspector (cb46b890b54f51f3a98c1935dbd50e143430757c5daf4080039d32865b04c1d5)
The package advertises itself as an 'HTTP probing tool for security researchers' but contains no HTTP-probing functionality. Its only behavior is to fetch and execute a Windows PE binary named 'mirai_agent.exe' from a hardcoded Tor hidden service (sytej5umomwukd77aantkxqj4aoke3kfist6eyne2pngavgsakum3iid.onion), with a localhost fallback. Two independent execution paths deliver the payload: (1) setup.py overrides the install command with a PostInstall class that spawns a background thread on `pip install` to download the binary, write it to a Microsoft-look-alike path under %TEMP%/MS/Update/agent.exe, set hidden+system file attributes via SetFileAttributesW, and launch it via CreateProcessW with CREATE_NO_WINDOW; (2) httpprobe/__init__.py exposes a main() that performs the same fetch-stage-hide-execute sequence at import time via CreateProcessW or subprocess.Popen. The duplicated install-time and import-time execution paths ensure code execution on the installer's Windows machine regardless of whether the package is installed or later imported by a consumer. The Microsoft-look-alike staging path, hidden+system attributes, no-window flag, and Tor-only delivery are all consistent with intent to persist an attacker-controlled binary on the developer's machine.

it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be

The package advertises itself as an 'HTTP probing tool for security researchers' but contains no HTTP-probing functionality. The duplicated install-time and import-time execution paths ensure code execution on the installer's Windows machine regardless of whether the package is installed or later imported by a consumer. The Microsoft-look-alike staging path, hidden+system attributes, no-window flag, and Tor-only delivery are all consistent with intent to persist an attacker-controlled binary on the developer's machine.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B shows a top similarity of 0.95 to apache-flink-libraries (unclassified), but also includes strypy tagged as 'typosquatting' at 0.95. This corroborates the Q1 anomaly.

happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR

neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious

underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,

reasoning.code_intent: Section A shows a setup.py script that gates execution on conditions (Compare, _is_root) and, when those gates evaluate false, performs a chain of obfuscated operations: base64.b64decode, chr, bytes, _ct.encode, _ct.rstrip, _d.decode, _p.communicate, and ctypes.windll.kernel32.SetFileAttributesW. reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B's top match is ninja-ssh-proto at 0.98 with specific tags backdoor, credential_stealer, data_exfiltration, obfuscated_payload, spyware_infostealer. reasoning.false_positive_reason: The specific anomaly is install-time decoding of string literals into executable content via base64.b64decode/chr/bytes and subprocess communication, combined with ctypes.windll.kernel32.SetFileAttributesW to hide files on Windows, gated by _is_root and false-evaluating Compare conditions. No documented config-toolkit functionality accounts for this behavior.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap in obfuscated payload decoding, process execution via subprocess communication, and install-time side effects. The matched sample carries confirmed backdoor, credential_stealer, data_exfiltration, obfuscated_payload, and spyware_infostealer tags, indicating the same low-level pattern was previously confirmed malicious.

policy_violations.violation_reason: The code decodes string literals and passes them to subprocess communication (_p.communicate) without sanitization, enabling execution of dynamically decoded content.
Dynamic decoding (base64.b64decode, chr, bytes) followed by execution via subprocess matches the obfuscated import/execution pattern this rule detects.

mitre_mapping.relevance: The use of subprocess communication and Windows file-attribute hiding (SetFileAttributesW) is consistent with evading process-tree-based analysis.
Decoded content executed via subprocess communication may be used to inject or run code in a separate process context.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.
